Propellers now burn what propellers burn

September 20, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

A full audit of all 197 aircraft went looking for two things: specs that did not match the real aircraft, and prices that made one choice obviously correct. The big finding was a propeller problem. Every turboprop and piston airliner in the game was burning roughly half to two-thirds of the fuel its real counterpart burns, while every jet was close to the real figure. The Q400 was the most fuel-efficient aircraft per seat in the entire catalogue — ahead of the A330neo, the A321XLR and the 787-9 — and a 1961 Vickers Vanguard was second.

  • Turboprop and piston fuel burn is now on the same scale as jets. Where real figures could be verified against engine data or published trip fuel — the Q400, the ATR 72-600, the Il-18 and the Vanguard — those numbers are used directly; the rest of the propeller fleet moved by the same proportion. A turboprop still beats a comparable regional jet on fuel, by the 20–35% it does in reality rather than the 40–45% it was managing here. The knock-on effect is that modern regional jets are worth flying again: the E195-E2 in particular goes from an also-ran to one of the strongest aircraft in the game on short, busy routes.
  • The 777X is finally a new aircraft. Both 777X variants were within about 1% of the 777s they replace on fuel per seat, which is not what a new engine and a new wing buy you. They now deliver the roughly 10% per seat they should, so upgrading is worth doing.
  • Aircraft whose production lines have closed no longer arrive factory-fresh. The A380, 747-8I, 777-200LR, E190, E195, CRJ-1000, SSJ100, An-148 and MA600 were all being delivered brand new from lines that shut years ago. They now arrive about as old as their line has been closed, which means a realistic maintenance bill from the first week rather than a brand-new one.
  • The Dash 7 is priced for what it can do. It is the only aircraft in the game carrying more than 40 seats that can use a runway under 3,100 feet, and it was leasing for less than a 40-seat Dash 8-200. That capability now costs what it is worth. It is still the right answer on a genuinely short field — it is simply no longer the cheapest way to do everything else as well.
  • Spec corrections. The 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 now enter service when they actually will rather than years ago, the A319neo’s service date is corrected, and the Yak-40, HS 748 and Stratocruiser carry their real certified seat counts. The 767-200SF was burning more fuel than the larger 767-300F, which is the wrong way round, and no longer does.
  • Six ranges corrected — and you will now be told when a route is out of reach. The DC-8-63 could fly further than the long-range DC-8-62 it was a stretch of, and the Il-96-300, An-148 and three freighters (the A330-200F, 767-200SF and DC-8-73F) were all carrying more range than the real aircraft. Until now, a route beyond its aircraft’s range simply stopped earning with no explanation at all while the aircraft kept costing you. That is fixed: a route that goes out of range gets a news item, a warning, and a red Out of range badge on the Routes and cargo pages naming the leg and the shortfall. Reassign it to a longer-range aircraft and it keeps its pricing and ramp-up — no relaunch cost. The same warning now also catches a cabin refit that costs a route its range.

Existing fleets keep the aircraft they have. Burn figures apply from this week, so a propeller fleet will see a higher fuel bill — if that changes the maths on a route, route economics explains how to read it, and every aircraft’s current figures are in the aircraft guide. If any of your routes are affected by the range corrections, you will see them in News the first time you load your save.
